<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">HIME: Mitigating Object Hallucinations in LVLMs via Hallucination Insensitivity Model Editing</h1>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Large Vision–Language Models (LVLMs) have demonstrated impressive multimodal understanding capabilities, yet they remain prone to object hallucination, where models describe non-existent objects or attribute incorrect factual information, raising serious concerns for reliable real-world deployment. While fine-tuning is a commonly adopted mitigation strategy, its high computational cost and practical difficulty motivate the need for training-free alternatives, among which model editing has recently emerged as a promising direction. However, indiscriminate editing risks disrupting the rich implicit knowledge encoded in pre-trained LVLMs, leading to a fundamental question: how much intervention is necessary at each layer to suppress hallucinations while preserving pre-trained knowledge?</p>
    
<p id="abstract1.2" class="ltx_p">To address this question, we present a systematic analysis of LVLM decoders built on three widely used large language model backbones—Qwen, LLaMA, and Vicuna—revealing clear layer-wise differences in susceptibility to object hallucination. Building on these insights, we introduce the Hallucination Insensitivity Score (HIS), a principled metric that quantifies each layer’s sensitivity to hallucination and provides guidance for targeted intervention. Leveraging HIS, we propose Hallucination Insensitivity Model Editing (HIME), a simple yet effective layer-adaptive weight editing approach that selectively modifies latent features to suppress hallucinations while preserving pre-trained knowledge. Extensive experiments demonstrate that HIME reduces hallucinations by an average of 61.8% across open-ended generation benchmarks, including CHAIR, MME, and GPT-4V-aided evaluation, without introducing additional parameters, inference-time latency, or computational overhead.</p>
  
</div>
<figure id="S0.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18711v1/HIME_adaptive_editing_v6.png" id="S0.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/342;" width="476" height="342" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S0.F1.7" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>: </span><span id="S0.F1.8" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Illustrates the phenomenon of knowledge distortion because of the fixed weight editing. On top, LVLM e.g. LLaVA-1.5 hallucinates non-existent objects, <span id="S0.F1.8.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#FF0000;">chair, couch</span>, frequently co-occurring to bed. Left bottom, Fixed Weight Editing reduce hallucinated object, yet drop existent objects, <span id="S0.F1.8.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#00FF00;">bed</span>. Right bottom, Our approach, HIME, mitigate hallucination, <span id="S0.F1.8.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#FF0000;">chair, couch</span>, and preserve the pre-trained knowledge, <span id="S0.F1.8.4" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#00FF00;">bed</span>.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Object hallucination remains a fundamental obstacle to the reliable deployment of Large Vision–Language Models
(LVLMs) in real-world settings <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al. (2024a)</a></cite>. While hallucination in Large Language Models (LLMs)
typically refers to the generation of unsupported or incorrect statements, hallucination in LVLMs is often
triggered by <em id="S1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">cross-modal misalignment</em>—the model produces objects or attributes that are not grounded
in the visual input <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ji et al. (2023)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al. (2023)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shi et al. (2023)</a></cite>. Such failures can compromise the
trustworthiness of multimodal systems in safety-critical or high-stakes scenarios, motivating the development
of effective mitigation strategies <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al. (2023)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhao et al. (2024)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang et al. (2024)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yue et al. (2024)</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Existing mitigation methods generally fall into two categories: <span id="S1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(i)</span> fine-tuning-based approaches
(e.g., preference optimisation and supervised adaptation) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xiao et al. (2025)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al. (2024)</a></cite>, and
<span id="S1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(ii)</span> training-free strategies <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Leng et al. (2024)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al. (2024b)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al. (2025)</a></cite>.
Although fine-tuning can be highly effective, it often requires curated supervision, careful engineering, and
substantial computation, which limits its practicality for rapid deployment and model updates. This has fuelled interest in training-free alternatives, including decoding-time interventions
(e.g., contrastive/auxiliary decoding)  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al. (2024)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Leng et al. (2024)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Deng et al. (2024)</a></cite> and offline
weight-editing methods <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al. (2025)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhuang et al. (2025)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al. (2025)</a></cite>. However, decoding-time methods typically incur additional inference cost and latency due to extra generation paths. Knowledge editing in LLMs has shown strong effectiveness; however, recent studies indicate that it can introduce undesirable side effects—such as knowledge distortion and knowledge conflict <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al. (2023b)</a></cite> —which remain under-explored in LVLM weight editing. As shown in Fig<a href="#S0.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ HIME: Mitigating Object Hallucinations in LVLMs via Hallucination Insensitivity Model Editing" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, LlaVA-1.5 model suffer from object hallucination, incorrectly describing non-existent objects, (e.g. <span id="S1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">“couch”, and “chair”</span>) that are frequently co-occurring to the object (<span id="S1.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">“bed”</span>). While Nullu <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al. (2025)</a></cite> applies a hard uniform weight editing that successfully removes the hallucinated object <span id="S1.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">“chair”</span>, it does so at the cost of suppressing the existent object <span id="S1.p2.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">“bed”</span>, indicating a distortion of factual visual knowledge. Therefore, uniform model editing introduces a potential risk: <em id="S1.p2.1.7" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">indiscriminate parameter modifications that can disrupt the implicit knowledge encoded in pre-trained LVLMs</em>. This raises a central question: <span id="S1.p2.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">to what extent should we intervene in each layer to suppress hallucination while preserving the model’s pre-trained knowledge?</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In this work, we show that object hallucination in Large Vision–Language Models (LVLMs) is not a uniform decoder-level phenomenon, but instead exhibits strong and systematic variation across layers. By conducting a layer-wise analysis of widely used LVLMs, LLaVA-1.5, QWen3-VL-8B-Instruct, QWen2-VL-8B-Instruct, MiniGPT-4, and mPLUG-Owl2—we uncover depth-dependent patterns in hallucination susceptibility that are consistent across architectures. This observation challenges the common practice <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al. (2025)</a></cite> of uniformly editing or regularising all decoder layers, which implicitly assumes equal contribution to hallucination and risks indiscriminately perturbing grounded visual representations and pre-trained semantic knowledge.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Building on these insights, we introduce the Hallucination Insensitivity
Score (HIS), a principled layer-level metric that quantifies how sensitive a layer is to hallucination and
therefore provides guidance for targeted intervention. Leveraging HIS, we propose
Hallucination Insensitivity Model Editing (HIME), a simple yet effective layer-adaptive weight
editing approach that selectively suppresses hallucination-related latent directions while preserving
pre-trained knowledge. Concretely, we derive attention-guided features for truthful and hallucinated samples,
estimate their contrastive discrepancy, and extract a low-rank hallucination subspace via Singular Value Decomposition (SVD). We then apply a
layer-adaptive weighted projection—controlled by Hallucination Insensitivity Score
to edit MLP weights offline, yielding an
edited LVLM that can be directly reloaded for inference with <em id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">zero</em> additional parameters, latency, or
computational overhead.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Extensive experiments show that HIME reduces hallucinations by an average of <math id="S1.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="61.8\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>61.8</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">61.8\%</annotation></semantics></math> across open-ended
generation benchmarks, including CHAIR, MME, and GPT-4V-aided evaluation, while maintaining overall model utility.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Our main contributions are:</p>
<ol id="S1.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We perform a layer-wise analysis of LVLM decoders and reveal that object hallucination LVLMs exhibit pronounced, depth-dependent susceptibility patterns, with certain layers consistently more prone to hallucination across architectures.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We introduce the Hallucination Insensitivity Score (HIS), a layer-level metric that quantifies hallucination susceptibility from internal decoder representations, and leverage it to develop Hallucination Insensitivity Model Editing (HIME), a training-free, layer-adaptive weight editing method for hallucination mitigation.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">3.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Across three LVLM backbones (LLaVA-1.5, MiniGPT-4, and mPLUG-Owl2) and multiple benchmarks, HIME consistently outperforms prior decoding- and editing-based approaches. HIME reduces object hallucination by an average of 61.8% on open-ended generation (CHAIR), while maintaining or improving BLEU and MME perception scores, with zero additional parameters, training, or inference-time overhead.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F2" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18711v1/GAME_main.png" id="S1.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/238;" width="476" height="238" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S1.F2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 2</span>: </span><span id="S1.F2.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">HIME hallucination mitigation framework.<span id="S1.F2.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Given an image with truthful and hallucinated captions, the Hallucination Insensitivity Score (HIS) is derived by contrasting attention distributions via KL divergence. During model editing , model weights are orthogonally projected into the truthful subspace and weighted by inverse HIS.
The resulting Edited LVLM Decoder emphasises truthful representations while reducing hallucination sensitivity across layers.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related Work</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Hallucination Mitigation in LVLMs:</span>
The recent adoption of advanced open-source large language models, including Llama <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Touvron et al. (2023)</a></cite>, Vicuna <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zheng et al. (2023)</a></cite>, and Qwen <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bai et al. (2023)</a></cite> has markedly enhanced LVLM performance, allowing them to tackle increasingly complex vision–language tasks. However, these models suffer from object hallucination when generate content inconsistent with the image (i.e., ungrounded), compounded by next-token training objectives that do not penalise unfaithful text. Benchmarks such as CHAIR <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rohrbach et al. (2018)</a></cite> has highlighted persistent grounding failures.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Various mitigation strategies have been proposed to mitigate hallucination in vision-language models. Mitigation strategies can be classified into three categories. (1) Contrastive Decoding, originally introduced in NLP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al. (2022)</a></cite>, has demonstrated effectiveness in reducing hallucination in LVLMs. The adoption of this technique has motivated a range of contrastive strategies such as VCD <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Leng et al. (2024)</a></cite>, and DoLa <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chuang et al. (2024)</a></cite>. While they achieve good performance, they incur heavy computational costs, particularly during training and fine-tuning.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In contrast to our training-free approach. (2) Feature Steering: contrast between the internal embeddings of positive and negative samples, and then edit the feature during the test-time to adjust the model’s response e.g. VTI <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al. (2024c)</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Although training-free, it lacks input adaptivity, as fixed shifts may be suboptimal across different scenes or prompts. (3) Null-Space Projection: leverages the null space projection for model editing. Nullu <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al. (2025)</a></cite> mitigates hallucinations by projecting contrastive latent features into the null space (HalluSpace), then orthogonalising the model weights to the null space. While effective, it applies fixed-weight editing to all layers, distorting the implicit model information. In contrast, our approach account for layer-wise susceptibility and applies layer-adaptive interventions that remove hallucination and preserve the pre-trained knowledge.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Method</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The overall framework is illustrated in Figure <a href="#S1.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ HIME: Mitigating Object Hallucinations in LVLMs via Hallucination Insensitivity Model Editing" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>. We first introduce preliminary concepts and notation used throughout the paper. We then present the Hallucination Insensitivity Score (HIS), which analyzes attention sensitivity across layers in recent LVLMs. Finally, we introduce Hallucination Insensitivity Model Editing (HIME), a method designed to mitigate object hallucination in LVLMs.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Preliminary</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Vision-Language Alignment.</span> The input to a vision-language foundation model (LVLM) consists of an image
<math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{I}^{(i)}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times C}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>𝐈</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>W</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{I}^{(i)}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times C}</annotation></semantics></math> and a textual query
<math id="S3.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s^{(i)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s^{(i)}</annotation></semantics></math>. A vision encoder (e.g., ViT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dosovitskiy et al. (2021)</a></cite>, CLIP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Radford et al. (2021)</a></cite>)
extracts visual features from <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{I}^{(i)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>𝐈</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{I}^{(i)}</annotation></semantics></math>, which are then mapped into the
language model embedding space via a vision–language alignment module
(e.g., Q-Former <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al. (2023a)</a></cite> or a linear projection). This
produces a sequence of <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> visual tokens</p>
<table id="S3.Ex1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{X}^{(i)}=[\mathbf{x}^{(i)}_{0},\mathbf{x}^{(i)}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{x}^{(i)}_{N-1}],\quad\mathbf{x}^{(i)}_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>𝐗</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>0</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{X}^{(i)}=[\mathbf{x}^{(i)}_{0},\mathbf{x}^{(i)}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{x}^{(i)}_{N-1}],\quad\mathbf{x}^{(i)}_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">The textual query <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q^{(i)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>q</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q^{(i)}</annotation></semantics></math> is tokenized into a sequence of <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> text tokens</p>
<table id="S3.Ex2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{T}^{(i)}=[\mathbf{t}^{(i)}_{0},\mathbf{t}^{(i)}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{t}^{(i)}_{M-1}],\quad\mathbf{t}^{(i)}_{m}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>𝐓</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐭</mi><mn>0</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐭</mi><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐭</mi><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐭</mi><mi>m</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{T}^{(i)}=[\mathbf{t}^{(i)}_{0},\mathbf{t}^{(i)}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{t}^{(i)}_{M-1}],\quad\mathbf{t}^{(i)}_{m}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.3" class="ltx_p">The combined multimodal input is formed by concatenation,
<math id="S3.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[\mathbf{X}^{(i)},\mathbf{T}^{(i)}]\in\mathbb{R}^{J\times d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msup><mi>𝐗</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>𝐓</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>J</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[\mathbf{X}^{(i)},\mathbf{T}^{(i)}]\in\mathbb{R}^{J\times d}</annotation></semantics></math>,
where <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J=N+M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>J</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J=N+M</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Model Forwarding.</span>
The concatenated token sequence is processed by the transformer backbone of
the LVLM. Let <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>L</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L</annotation></semantics></math> denote the total number of transformer layers, and let
<math id="S3.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{z}_{\ell,j}^{(i)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐳</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{z}_{\ell,j}^{(i)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the hidden representation of
token index <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j\in\{0,\dots,J-1\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>J</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j\in\{0,\dots,J-1\}</annotation></semantics></math> at layer <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell\in\{1,\dots,L\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell\in\{1,\dots,L\}</annotation></semantics></math> for sample
<math id="S3.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>. The model produces a set of contextualized token representations</p>
<table id="S3.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\left\{\mathbf{z}_{\ell,j}^{(i)}\right\}_{\ell=1,j=0}^{L,\,J-1}=f_{\theta}^{\text{LVLM}}\!\left(\mathbf{I}^{(i)},s^{(i)}\right)." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mo>{</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐳</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>}</mo></mrow><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo rspace="0.337em">,</mo><mrow><mi>J</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi><mtext>LVLM</mtext></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>𝐈</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\left\{\mathbf{z}_{\ell,j}^{(i)}\right\}_{\ell=1,j=0}^{L,\,J-1}=f_{\theta}^{\text{LVLM}}\!\left(\mathbf{I}^{(i)},s^{(i)}\right).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.2" class="ltx_p">These hidden states jointly encode visual and linguistic context and form the
basis for downstream reasoning and response generation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Response Generation.</span>
Following the forward pass, response generation is performed in an
autoregressive manner. At decoding step <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>, the probability distribution over
the next token <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y_{t+1}^{(i)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>y</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y_{t+1}^{(i)}</annotation></semantics></math> is computed from the final-layer hidden
representation corresponding to the current decoding position,</p>
<table id="S3.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E2.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="P\!\left(y_{t+1}^{(i)}\mid y_{1:t}^{(i)},\mathbf{z}_{L,0:J-1}^{(i)}\right)=\text{softmax}\!\left(\mathbf{W}_{o}\,\mathbf{z}_{L,j_{t}}^{(i)}\right)," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mpadded style="width:0.611em;" width="0.611em"><mi>P</mi></mpadded><mrow><mo>(</mo><msubsup><mi>y</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><msubsup><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐳</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi>J</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mpadded style="width:3.720em;" width="3.720em"><mtext>softmax</mtext></mpadded><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>o</mi></msub><msubsup><mi>𝐳</mi><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>j</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P\!\left(y_{t+1}^{(i)}\mid y_{1:t}^{(i)},\mathbf{z}_{L,0:J-1}^{(i)}\right)=\text{softmax}\!\left(\mathbf{W}_{o}\,\mathbf{z}_{L,j_{t}}^{(i)}\right),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p3.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>j</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> indexes the token position at step <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>, and
<math id="S3.SS1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}_{o}\in\mathbb{R}^{V\times d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>o</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}_{o}\in\mathbb{R}^{V\times d}</annotation></semantics></math> is the output projection matrix for a
vocabulary of size <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>V</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V</annotation></semantics></math>. Decoding proceeds until an end-of-sequence token is
generated or a predefined maximum length is reached.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F3" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18711v1/models_his_plot.svg" id="S3.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_portrait" style="aspect-ratio:476/641;" width="476" height="641"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F3.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 3</span>: </span><span id="S3.F3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Layer-wise distribution of the Hallucination Insensitivity Score (HIS) across four VLM backbones. The y-axis reports the HIS value (higher indicates greater robustness to hallucinations). Across four VLM decoders, we observe a highly structured, non-uniform depth profile. Across architectures, mid-depth layers exhibit consistently higher robustness, while late/early decoder layers show pronounced sensitivity to hallucinations. This recurring pattern suggests targeted editing of specific depth regions rather than global model intervention.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>LVLM Attention Behaviour</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al. (2025)</a></cite> strategy, we utilise the contrastive dataset LURE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al. (2024)</a></cite> that contain vision-language pairs in which each image is associated with two different captions: one hallucinated and one truthful ground truth. We denote <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{i}^{+}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{i}^{+}</annotation></semantics></math> as the ground-truth sample that precisely describes the image contents, and <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{i}^{-}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>−</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{i}^{-}</annotation></semantics></math> as the hallucinated sample whose caption contains hallucinated descriptions. The whole dataset can be denoted as <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}=(x_{i}^{+},x_{i}^{-})_{i=1}^{N}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>−</mo></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}=(x_{i}^{+},x_{i}^{-})_{i=1}^{N}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">GPT-3.5 is employed to transform the accurate captions into the hallucinated counterparts, as described in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al. (2024)</a></cite>. These transformations are driven by factors implicated in object hallucination co-occurrence statistics, uncertainty of object existence, and positional placement within the caption. Thereafter, we obtain paired samples by replacing objects in the ground-truth description with their most probable hallucinated counterparts, resulting in an image paired with both the ground-truth and the hallucinated descriptions.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">LVLM Hallucination Insensitivity Score (HIS).</span> LVLMs rely on a Transformer-based LLM decoder that generates text using attention mechanisms. Consequently, the importance of each token depends on how much attention it receives across the layers during decoding. To systematically investigate how LVLMs respond to the input tokens during response generation, we introduce a <span id="S3.SS2.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Hallucination Insensitivity Score</span> which is a distributional distance measure that quantifies and tracks, across layer, the degree of attention sensitivity between truthful and hallucinated tokens during the decoding process. This layer-adaptive metric of hallucination susceptibility is used to guide targeted, selective interventions.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Formally, we fed both the truthful, <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{i}^{+}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{i}^{+}</annotation></semantics></math>, and hallucinated, <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{i}^{-}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>−</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{i}^{-}</annotation></semantics></math>, samples to the LVLM, and calculate the attention matrix over each head for both of them using the following equation:</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<table id="S3.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{A}^{(h)}\;=\;\mathrm{Softmax}\!\left(\frac{\mathbf{Q}^{(h)}{\mathbf{K}^{(h)}}^{\!\top}}{\sqrt{d_{k}/H}}\right)\mathbf{V}^{(h)}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>𝐀</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0.558em" rspace="0.558em">=</mo><mrow><mrow><mpadded style="width:3.922em;" width="3.922em"><mi>Softmax</mi></mpadded><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mfrac><mrow><msup><mi>𝐐</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mmultiscripts><mi>𝐊</mi><mrow></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow></mrow><mo>⊤</mo></mmultiscripts></mrow><msqrt><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>/</mo><mi>H</mi></mrow></msqrt></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>𝐕</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{A}^{(h)}\;=\;\mathrm{Softmax}\!\left(\frac{\mathbf{Q}^{(h)}{\mathbf{K}^{(h)}}^{\!\top}}{\sqrt{d_{k}/H}}\right)\mathbf{V}^{(h)}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p6.1" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS2.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>h</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math> is the head number, <math id="S3.SS2.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{k}</annotation></semantics></math> represents embedding dimension, <math id="S3.SS2.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>H</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H</annotation></semantics></math> is the numbrer of attention head, and <math id="S3.SS2.p6.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{Q},\mathbf{K},\mathbf{V}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐐</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝐊</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝐕</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{Q},\mathbf{K},\mathbf{V}</annotation></semantics></math> represent Query, Key, and Value, respectively.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p7" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p7.1" class="ltx_p">For simplicity, we average attention scores across heads using <math id="S3.SS2.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{\mathbf{A}}^{+}_{l}=\frac{1}{H}\sum_{h=1}^{H}\mathbf{A}^{+}_{l,h},\;\;\bar{\mathbf{A}}^{+}_{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{J\times J}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐀</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mi>l</mi><mo>+</mo></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>H</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>H</mi></msubsup><msubsup><mi>𝐀</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo></msubsup></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.727em">,</mo><mrow><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐀</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mi>l</mi><mo>+</mo></msubsup><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>J</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>J</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{\mathbf{A}}^{+}_{l}=\frac{1}{H}\sum_{h=1}^{H}\mathbf{A}^{+}_{l,h},\;\;\bar{\mathbf{A}}^{+}_{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{J\times J}</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S3.SS2.p7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>J</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J</annotation></semantics></math> is length of all tokens, to derive a single layer-level attention matrix over all tokens, <math id="S3.SS2.p7.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{\mathbf{A}}^{+}_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐀</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mi>l</mi><mo>+</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{\mathbf{A}}^{+}_{l}</annotation></semantics></math> and similarly, for <math id="S3.SS2.p7.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{\mathbf{A}}^{-}_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐀</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mi>l</mi><mo>−</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{\mathbf{A}}^{-}_{l}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.SS2.p7.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell\in\{1,\dots,L\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell\in\{1,\dots,L\}</annotation></semantics></math>. Because each token distributes attention across the entire sequence, we require a representation that preserves meaningful token-level variability. One option is to average attention over tokens; however, this implicitly weights all tokens equally, despite substantial disparities in their attention magnitudes. To address this, we propose a distributional divergence that characterizes the overall attention behaviour. Specifically, for each layer <math id="S3.SS2.p7.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>l</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l</annotation></semantics></math>, we flatten
<math id="S3.SS2.p7.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{\mathbf{A}}^{+}_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐀</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mi>l</mi><mo>+</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{\mathbf{A}}^{+}_{l}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS2.p7.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{\mathbf{A}}^{-}_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐀</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mi>l</mi><mo>−</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{\mathbf{A}}^{-}_{l}</annotation></semantics></math> to get a vector of attention scores <math id="S3.SS2.p7.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{a}^{+}_{l}=\mathrm{vec}\!\left(\bar{\mathbf{A}}^{+}_{l}\right)\in\mathbb{R}^{J^{2}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐚</mi><mi>l</mi><mo>+</mo></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mpadded style="width:1.249em;" width="1.249em"><mi>vec</mi></mpadded><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐀</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mi>l</mi><mo>+</mo></msubsup><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msup><mi>J</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{a}^{+}_{l}=\mathrm{vec}\!\left(\bar{\mathbf{A}}^{+}_{l}\right)\in\mathbb{R}^{J^{2}}</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S3.SS2.p7.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{a}^{-}_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐚</mi><mi>l</mi><mo>−</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{a}^{-}_{l}</annotation></semantics></math>, then map both of them into a histogram <math id="S3.SS2.p7.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p^{+}_{\ell}=[a^{+}_{0,l},a^{+}_{1,l},\cdots,a^{+}_{B,l}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>p</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>+</mo></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋯</mo><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo></msubsup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p^{+}_{\ell}=[a^{+}_{0,l},a^{+}_{1,l},\cdots,a^{+}_{B,l}]</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS2.p7.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q^{-}_{\ell}=[a^{-}_{0,l},a^{-}_{1,l},\cdots,a^{-}_{B,l}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>q</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>−</mo></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋯</mo><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo></msubsup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q^{-}_{\ell}=[a^{-}_{0,l},a^{-}_{1,l},\cdots,a^{-}_{B,l}]</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.SS2.p7.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{i},q_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{B}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>B</mi></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{i},q_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{B}</annotation></semantics></math> with <math id="S3.SS2.p7.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>B</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B</annotation></semantics></math> bins.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p8.1" class="ltx_p">We then quantify layer-wise hallucination sensitivity via KL divergence, where <math id="S3.SS2.p8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>b</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b</annotation></semantics></math> indexes histogram bins.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p9" class="ltx_para">
<table id="S3.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E4.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathrm{HIS}_{\ell}\;=\;D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\ell\,\|\,q_{\ell})\;=\;\sum_{b=1}^{B}p_{l,b}\log\frac{p_{l,b}}{q_{l,b}}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>HIS</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.558em" rspace="0.558em">=</mo><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>KL</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0.337em">∥</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo rspace="0.280em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.391em">=</mo><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>B</mi></munderover><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></msub><mi>log</mi><mfrac><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi>q</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></msub></mfrac><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{HIS}_{\ell}\;=\;D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\ell\,\|\,q_{\ell})\;=\;\sum_{b=1}^{B}p_{l,b}\log\frac{p_{l,b}}{q_{l,b}}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p10" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p10.1" class="ltx_p">We introduce <span id="S3.SS2.p10.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Hallucination Insensitivity Score</span> (HIS) to quantify, at each decoder layer, how separable the attention behaviour is between truthful and hallucinated generations. A larger HIS implies a greater divergence between the two attention distributions, indicating that the layer can more clearly discriminate hallucinated from truthful outputs. Conversely, a smaller HIS reflects highly similar distributions, suggesting limited sensitivity (i.e., potential confusion) and therefore highlighting the layer as a suitable target for focused intervention or repair, see Figure <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 3.1 Preliminary ‣ 3 Method ‣ HIME: Mitigating Object Hallucinations in LVLMs via Hallucination Insensitivity Model Editing" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Hallucination Insensitivity Model Editing</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The internal outputs such as hidden states and self-attention maps are contextualised representations that jointly capture the model’s reasoning and generation ability, but they also entangle signals related to language hallucination <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Vaswani et al. (2017)</a></cite>. Consequently, relying on hidden states alone is often insufficient for isolating the hallucination subspaces <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al. (2025)</a></cite>. We therefore leverage layer-wise attention to derive more informative and guided hidden representations, which we then use to identify and suppress hallucination subspaces.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Layer-wise attention-guided representations.</span> Formally, for each layer <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell</annotation></semantics></math> in the LVLM backbone, where <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell\in\{1,\dots,L\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell\in\{1,\dots,L\}</annotation></semantics></math>, we extract contextual embedding features for both truthful and hallucinated samples, denoted as <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E^{+}_{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>E</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>+</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E^{+}_{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E^{-}_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times J\times D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>E</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>−</mo></msubsup><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>J</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E^{-}_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times J\times D}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> number of samples, <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>J</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J</annotation></semantics></math> sequence length, and <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>D</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math> MLP embedding dimension. Unlike prior methods <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al. (2025)</a></cite> that rely solely on hidden states, we additionally leverage layer-wise attention to obtain more informative and guided representations. Specifically, for each contrastive sample, we compute the per-layer attention matrices <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A^{+}_{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>+</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A^{+}_{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A^{-}_{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>−</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A^{-}_{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math> using Eq. <a href="#S3.E3" title="In 3.2 LVLM Attention Behaviour ‣ 3 Method ‣ HIME: Mitigating Object Hallucinations in LVLMs via Hallucination Insensitivity Model Editing" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>. We then normalise the attention per head and average across heads to obtain a single layer-level attention matrix <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{A}^{+}_{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>A</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>+</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{A}^{+}_{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{A}^{-}_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{J\times J}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>A</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>−</mo></msubsup><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>J</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>J</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{A}^{-}_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{J\times J}</annotation></semantics></math> for both truthful and hallucinated samples, respectively.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">To derive a one-dimensional positional importance distribution, we aggregate <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{A}_{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>A</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{A}_{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math> over the <em id="S3.SS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">key</em> dimension: <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\pi}_{\ell}[q]\;=\;\frac{1}{J}\sum_{k=1}^{J}\bar{A}_{\ell}[q,k]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝝅</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>q</mi><mo rspace="0.280em" stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.558em">=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>J</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>J</mi></msubsup><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>A</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\pi}_{\ell}[q]\;=\;\frac{1}{J}\sum_{k=1}^{J}\bar{A}_{\ell}[q,k]</annotation></semantics></math> Consequently, <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\pi}_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{J}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝝅</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>J</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\pi}_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{J}</annotation></semantics></math> is a 1D positional distribution of length <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>J</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J</annotation></semantics></math> that assigns,
for each query position, its average attention mass allocated across all keys at layer <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Using the hidden embeddings at layer <math id="S3.SS3.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.SS3.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E^{+}_{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>E</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>+</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E^{+}_{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS3.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E^{-}_{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>E</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>−</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E^{-}_{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math>, we combine them with the
positional attention distribution <math id="S3.SS3.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{p}_{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐩</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{p}_{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math> to obtain an attention-weighted expectation of the
hidden states. Specifically, we compute
<math id="S3.SS3.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{Z}^{+}_{\ell}\;=\;{\mathbf{p}^{+}_{\ell}}E^{+}_{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐙</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>+</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0.558em" rspace="0.558em">=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐩</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>+</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>E</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>+</mo></msubsup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{Z}^{+}_{\ell}\;=\;{\mathbf{p}^{+}_{\ell}}E^{+}_{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math> and
<math id="S3.SS3.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{Z}^{-}_{\ell}\;=\;{\bm{\pi}^{-}_{\ell}}E^{-}_{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐙</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>−</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0.558em" rspace="0.558em">=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝝅</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>−</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>E</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>−</mo></msubsup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{Z}^{-}_{\ell}\;=\;{\bm{\pi}^{-}_{\ell}}E^{-}_{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math>,
yielding attention-guided features for truthful and hallucinated generations, respectively, where
<math id="S3.SS3.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{Z}^{+}_{\ell},\mathbf{Z}^{-}_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐙</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>+</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐙</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>−</mo></msubsup><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{Z}^{+}_{\ell},\mathbf{Z}^{-}_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times D}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.SS3.p4.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>D</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the LLM embedding dimension and <math id="S3.SS3.p4.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> is the number of samples.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.p5.1" class="ltx_p">To characterise the latent discrepancy between truthful and hallucinated embeddings in the feature space, we
compute a layer-wise difference matrix at layer <math id="S3.SS3.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="S3.E5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{Z}_{\ell}\;=\;\mathbf{Z}^{+}_{\ell}-\mathbf{Z}^{-}_{\ell},\qquad\mathbf{Z}_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times D}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝐙</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.558em" rspace="0.558em">=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐙</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>+</mo></msubsup><mo>−</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐙</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>−</mo></msubsup></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="2.167em">,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐙</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{Z}_{\ell}\;=\;\mathbf{Z}^{+}_{\ell}-\mathbf{Z}^{-}_{\ell},\qquad\mathbf{Z}_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times D}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(5)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS3.p5.2" class="ltx_p">We then apply singular value decomposition (SVD) to obtain a low-rank factorisation of <math id="S3.SS3.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{Z}_{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐙</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{Z}_{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math>,
thereby capturing the dominant directions that separate truthful from hallucinated features. These principal
directions define a compact subspace that can be leveraged to suppress hallucination-related components in
the model representations:</p>
<table id="S3.E6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{Z}_{\ell}=\mathbf{U}_{\ell}\,\bm{\Sigma}_{\ell}\,\mathbf{V}_{\ell}^{\top},\qquad\mathbf{U}_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N},\;\mathbf{V}_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times D}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝐙</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐔</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝚺</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐕</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="2.167em">,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐔</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><mo rspace="0.447em">,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐕</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{Z}_{\ell}=\mathbf{U}_{\ell}\,\bm{\Sigma}_{\ell}\,\mathbf{V}_{\ell}^{\top},\qquad\mathbf{U}_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N},\;\mathbf{V}_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times D}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(6)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS3.p5.3" class="ltx_p">Here, <math id="S3.SS3.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\Sigma}_{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝚺</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\Sigma}_{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math> is a diagonal matrix whose entries are the singular values sorted in
descending order. We select the top-<math id="S3.SS3.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> right singular vectors
<math id="S3.SS3.p5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{v}^{\ell}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{v}^{\ell}_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐯</mi><mn>1</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐯</mi><mi>k</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{v}^{\ell}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{v}^{\ell}_{k}</annotation></semantics></math> (the first <math id="S3.SS3.p5.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> columns of <math id="S3.SS3.p5.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{V}_{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐕</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{V}_{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math>), which
capture the most salient directions of discrepancy between truthful and hallucinated features. We stack these
vectors to form <math id="S3.SS3.p5.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{V}_{\ell,k}\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐕</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{V}_{\ell,k}\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times k}</annotation></semantics></math> and regard their span as the <em id="S3.SS3.p5.3.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">hallucination
subspace</em> at layer <math id="S3.SS3.p5.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS3.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Weighted model editing.</span>
Let <math id="S3.SS3.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{V}_{\ell,k}\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐕</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{V}_{\ell,k}\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times k}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the top-<math id="S3.SS3.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> right singular vectors at layer <math id="S3.SS3.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell</annotation></semantics></math>,
and define the hallucination projector
<math id="S3.SS3.p6.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{V}_{\ell,k}\mathbf{V}_{\ell,k}^{\top}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐕</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐕</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{V}_{\ell,k}\mathbf{V}_{\ell,k}^{\top}</annotation></semantics></math>.
We modulate the intervention strength using the complement score <math id="S3.SS3.p6.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="HIS^{c}_{\ell}\in[0,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>I</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>c</mi></msubsup></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">HIS^{c}_{\ell}\in[0,1]</annotation></semantics></math>, yielding the
<em id="S3.SS3.p6.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">weighted null-space operator</em></p>
<table id="S3.E7" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{N}_{\ell}\;=\;\mathbf{I}-\text{HIS}^{c}_{\ell}\mathbf{V}_{\ell,k}\mathbf{V}_{\ell,k}^{\top}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝐍</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.558em" rspace="0.558em">=</mo><mrow><mi>𝐈</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><msubsup><mtext>HIS</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>c</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐕</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐕</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{N}_{\ell}\;=\;\mathbf{I}-\text{HIS}^{c}_{\ell}\mathbf{V}_{\ell,k}\mathbf{V}_{\ell,k}^{\top}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(7)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS3.p6.2" class="ltx_p">Compared to prior work <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al. (2025)</a></cite>, which applies the full projection
<math id="S3.SS3.p6.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{P}_{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐈</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>𝐏</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{P}_{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math> and may induce abrupt parameter changes, Eq. <a href="#S3.E7" title="In 3.3 Hallucination Insensitivity Model Editing ‣ 3 Method ‣ HIME: Mitigating Object Hallucinations in LVLMs via Hallucination Insensitivity Model Editing" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> provides a
smooth interpolation from <em id="S3.SS3.p6.2.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">no editing</em> (<math id="S3.SS3.p6.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="HIS^{c}_{\ell}=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>I</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>c</mi></msubsup></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">HIS^{c}_{\ell}=0</annotation></semantics></math>) to <em id="S3.SS3.p6.2.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">full projection</em> (<math id="S3.SS3.p6.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="HIS^{c}_{\ell}=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>I</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>c</mi></msubsup></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">HIS^{c}_{\ell}=1</annotation></semantics></math>)</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p7" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.p7.1" class="ltx_p">We then edit the MLP weights by applying <math id="S3.SS3.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{N}_{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐍</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{N}_{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math> on the appropriate side:</p>
<table id="S3.E8" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}^{\mathrm{ed}}_{\ell}\;=\;\mathbf{N}_{\ell}\mathbf{W}^{\mathrm{org}}_{\ell},\qquad" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐖</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>ed</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0.558em" rspace="0.558em">=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐍</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐖</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>org</mi></msubsup></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}^{\mathrm{ed}}_{\ell}\;=\;\mathbf{N}_{\ell}\mathbf{W}^{\mathrm{org}}_{\ell},\qquad</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(8)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS3.p7.2" class="ltx_p">At inference time, we replace <math id="S3.SS3.p7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}^{\mathrm{org}}_{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐖</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>org</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}^{\mathrm{org}}_{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math> with <math id="S3.SS3.p7.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}^{\mathrm{ed}}_{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐖</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>ed</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}^{\mathrm{ed}}_{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math>, enabling
hallucination mitigation without introducing additional parameters, latency, or computational overhead, since
the edited weights can be directly reloaded into the LVLM.</p>
</div>
