<td id="S3.T1.3.1.2.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t" style="padding:0.5pt 4.0pt;"><math id="S3.T1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{CHAIR}_{i}\downarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mtext>CHAIR</mtext><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">↓</mo><mphantom></mphantom></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{CHAIR}_{i}\downarrow</annotation></semantics></math></td>

Lower <math id="S3.T1.m102" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{CHAIR}_{s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mtext>CHAIR</mtext><mi>s</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{CHAIR}_{s}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.T1.m103" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{CHAIR}_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mtext>CHAIR</mtext><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{CHAIR}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> indicate less Object Hallucination. </div>

              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l6.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">6:</span></span>
              
              
              Compute positional attention distributions over <em id="alg1.l6.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">keys</em> (column mean):
<math id="alg1.l6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\pi}^{+}_{\ell}[k]\leftarrow\frac{1}{J}\sum_{q=1}^{J}\bar{A}^{+}_{\ell}[q,k]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝝅</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>+</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>J</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>J</mi></msubsup><mrow><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>A</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>+</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\pi}^{+}_{\ell}[k]\leftarrow\frac{1}{J}\sum_{q=1}^{J}\bar{A}^{+}_{\ell}[q,k]</annotation></semantics></math>  and 
<math id="alg1.l6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\pi}^{-}_{\ell}[k]\leftarrow\frac{1}{J}\sum_{q=1}^{J}\bar{A}^{-}_{\ell}[q,k]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝝅</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>−</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>J</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>J</mi></msubsup><mrow><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>A</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>−</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\pi}^{-}_{\ell}[k]\leftarrow\frac{1}{J}\sum_{q=1}^{J}\bar{A}^{-}_{\ell}[q,k]</annotation></semantics></math>

              Attention-weighted features:
<math id="alg1.l7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{Z}^{+}_{\ell}\leftarrow\bm{\pi}^{+}_{\ell}E^{+}_{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐙</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>+</mo></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝝅</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>+</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>E</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>+</mo></msubsup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{Z}^{+}_{\ell}\leftarrow\bm{\pi}^{+}_{\ell}E^{+}_{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math>, 
<math id="alg1.l7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{Z}^{-}_{\ell}\leftarrow\bm{\pi}^{-}_{\ell}E^{-}_{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐙</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>−</mo></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝝅</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>−</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>E</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>−</mo></msubsup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{Z}^{-}_{\ell}\leftarrow\bm{\pi}^{-}_{\ell}E^{-}_{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math>,

<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Experimental Setup</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we briefly introduce the baselines and the standard benchmarks used to evaluate the object hallucination of LVLMs, implementation details in Appendix. We take the average of three experiments.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">

<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Baselines:</span> To evaluate the effectiveness and generalisation of our approach in reducing the object hallucination, we utilise three representative LVLMs, including LLaVA-1.5 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al. (2023)</a></cite>, MiniGPT-4 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhu et al. (2023)</a></cite>, and mPLUG-Owl2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ye et al. (2024)</a></cite>, and two advanced LVLMs with different LLM architecture other than LLaMA Qwen2-VL-8B-Instruct <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al. (2024a)</a></cite>, and Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bai et al. (2025)</a></cite>. Check the appendix for more implementation details.</p>

We evaluate our method on the commonly used datasets for LVLMs hallucination mitigation: CHAIR <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rohrbach et al. (2018)</a></cite>, LLaVA-Bench <span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
              
              
              
            https://huggingface.co/datasets/liuhaotian/llavabench-in-the-wild</span></span></span>, and MME <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yin et al. (2024a)</a></cite>, due to page limit we moved datasets details to appendix.</p>
</div>

</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Evaluation and Results</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This section reports experimental results demonstrating our Hallucination Insensitivity Model Editing in mitigating the object hallucination in LVLMs.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.1 </span>Results on CHAIR</h3>

<div id="S5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As shown in Table <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 3.3 Hallucination Insensitivity Model Editing ‣ 3 Method ‣ HIME: Mitigating Object Hallucinations in LVLMs via Hallucination Insensitivity Model Editing" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, HIME achieves significant hallucination reduction for open-ended generation, outperforming the existing inference-time, contrastive decoding, and model editing approaches across the three models LLaVA1.5, MiiniGPT-4, and mPLUG-Owl2. Moreover, our approach, HIME, improves the state-of-the-art Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct, and Qwen2-VL-8B-Instruct models’ ability to mitigate hallucination, while preserving models’ implicit knowledge, as shown in Table <a href="#S3.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 3.3 Hallucination Insensitivity Model Editing ‣ 3 Method ‣ HIME: Mitigating Object Hallucinations in LVLMs via Hallucination Insensitivity Model Editing" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>.
The CHAIR<sub id="S5.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_sub"><span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">s</span></sub> (C<sub id="S5.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_sub"><span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">s</span></sub>) metric is very critical as a caption is counted as an error if it contains even a single hallucinated object, regardless of how many correct objects it mentions. Consequently, a substantial improvement in CHAIR<sub id="S5.SS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_sub"><span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">s</span></sub> indicates that our approach is effective at eliminating the remaining hallucinations and making more captions entirely hallucination-free.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F5" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18711v1/chair_bleu_kl_comparison_6.svg" id="S5.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/314;" width="476" height="314"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S5.F5.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 5</span>: </span><span id="S5.F5.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Ablation study evaluation results for Hallucination Insensitivity Score (HIS) on LLaVA-1.5. Lower CHAIR<sub id="S5.F5.6.1" class="ltx_sub"><span id="S5.F5.6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">s</span></sub>, and CHAIR<sub id="S5.F5.6.2" class="ltx_sub"><span id="S5.F5.6.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">i</span></sub> is better, while higher BLUE is better.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.2 </span>Results on MME</h3>

<div id="S5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To evaluate the overall performance of the proposed method, we report the results of the LLaVA-1.5-7B model as a representative case. Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 4.1 Baselines and Datasets ‣ 4 Experimental Setup ‣ HIME: Mitigating Object Hallucinations in LVLMs via Hallucination Insensitivity Model Editing" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> shows that employing HIME consistently boosts the performance of the baseline LLaVA-1.5 model on perception tasks such as Count, Position, and Celebrity. Notably, HIME also achieves superior results outperforming the state-of-the-art approach, Nullu, with a large margin in all of the tasks, except the Colour task. HIME consistently boosts performance on perception-based tasks without degrading the models’ original recognition abilities. We attribute this to HIME’s ability to reduce statistical biases and language priors, yielding more visually grounded reasoning and, in turn, stronger overall perception. Moreover, we employed our approach with two other models MiniGPT-4 and mPLUG-Owl2, check the appendix, HIME has boosted the baseline performance significantly.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F6" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18711v1/LLaVA_vs_Nullu_vs_GAME_gpt4v_evaluation_performance_comparison_9.svg" id="S5.F6.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/353;" width="476" height="353"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S5.F6.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 6</span>: </span><span id="S5.F6.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Results from a GPT-4V–assisted evaluation of open-ended generation. Accuracy reflects how well the response matches the image, while Detailedness captures the richness of relevant detail. Both scores are reported on a 10-point scale. on LLaVA-1.5.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.3 </span>GPT-4V Aided Evaluation on LLaVA-Bench.</h3>

<div id="S5.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our analysis was broadened to include the open-ended captioning tasks within the LLaVA-Bench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al. (2024b)</a></cite>, leveraging the capabilities of the recently released GPT-4V <span id="footnote2" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">2</span>
              
              
              
            https://openai.com/research/gpt-4v-system-card</span></span></span> following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al. (2025)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Leng et al. (2024)</a></cite>. Figure <a href="#S5.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ 5.2 Results on MME ‣ 5 Evaluation and Results ‣ HIME: Mitigating Object Hallucinations in LVLMs via Hallucination Insensitivity Model Editing" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> shows a consistent enhancement in HIME’s performance over the state-of-the-art and the baseline LLaVA model. The observed improvement in accuracy points to HIME’s capability to reduce hallucinations efficiently. Simultaneously, HIME’s presents a better detailedness of the responses than Nullu but slightly less than the baseline. More qualitative studies are included in the appendix.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Hallucination Sensitivity Score:</span> measures, for each layer, how sensitive attention is to factual versus hallucinated captions across the full generation process. We then use it to softly weight the magnitude of layer updates during editing. Importantly, it is not a tunable hyperparameter; it is computed once and requires no optimization. Nevertheless, we include an ablation to assess the impact of using this metric during model editing. As illustrated in Figure <a href="#S5.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 5.1 Results on CHAIR ‣ 5 Evaluation and Results ‣ HIME: Mitigating Object Hallucinations in LVLMs via Hallucination Insensitivity Model Editing" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, applying smooth, layer-wise updates markedly improves performance. This suggests that rigid weight edits can discard valuable prior knowledge, which is essential for accurate generation.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this work, we tackled object hallucination in LVLMs by proposing Hallucination Insensitivity Model Editing (HIME). Based on a systematic analysis of layer-wise behavior across LVLMs built on Qwen, LLaMA, and Vicuna, we showed that hallucination susceptibility varies across layers. We introduced the Hallucination Insensitivity Score (HIS) to quantify this layer-wise sensitivity and to guide targeted intervention. Building on HIS, HIME performs layer-adaptive weight editing by selectively modifying models’ weights to suppress hallucinations while preserving the model’s pre-trained knowledge. Extensive evaluations demonstrate consistent hallucination reduction across benchmarks, without introducing additional parameters, inference-time latency, or computational overhead.</p>
</div>
</section>

<div id="p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="p1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center"><span id="p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:173%;">Supplementary Material for
<br class="ltx_break">HIME: Mitigating Object Hallucinations in LVLMs via Hallucination Insensitivity Model Editing</span></p>

<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>LVLM Hallucination Insensitivity Score</h2>

<div id="A1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As shown in Figure <a href="#A3.F10" title="Figure 10 ‣ C.2 LLaVA-Bench and GPT-4V prompt ‣ Appendix C Extended Evaluation ‣ HIME: Mitigating Object Hallucinations in LVLMs via Hallucination Insensitivity Model Editing" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>, we extend the analysis with layer-wise distribution of the Hallucination Insensitivity Score (HIS) across three widely used LLMs backbones Vicuna, LlaMA-2, representing five widely used LVLMs: LLaVA-1.5, MiniGP), mPLUG-Owl2, Qwen2-VL, and recently proposed Qwen3-VL. Despite architectural differences, the models exhibit broadly consistent layer-wise trends, with certain layers appearing more susceptible to hallucination while others remain comparatively robust. These observations support HIS as a principled signal for identifying hallucination-prone layers and guiding targeted model editing. Note that MiniGPT-4, LLaVA-1.5, and mPLUG-Owl2 employ 32 decoder layers, whereas Qwen3-VL uses 36 layers, and Qwen2-Vl uses 28 layers.</p>
</div>
<section id="A1.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.1 </span>Ablation Study - Extended</h3>

<div id="A1.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Effects of editing layers:</span> HIME has two primary parameters: the set of layer indices to edit <math id="A1.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>l</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l</annotation></semantics></math> and the number of top-<math id="A1.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> singular vectors in the null space selected. We evaluate various settings of these hyperparameters on LLaVA-1.5-7B using the CHAIR benchmark. As shown in Table <a href="#A1.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ A.1 Ablation Study - Extended ‣ Appendix A LVLM Hallucination Insensitivity Score ‣ HIME: Mitigating Object Hallucinations in LVLMs via Hallucination Insensitivity Model Editing" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, the number of edited layers has an impact on the model’s overall performance, which varies across models. Thus, in this ablation study, to assess the impact of <math id="A1.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>l</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l</annotation></semantics></math> on the model performance, we fixed <math id="A1.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> to 5.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">As summarised in Table <a href="#A1.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ A.1 Ablation Study - Extended ‣ Appendix A LVLM Hallucination Insensitivity Score ‣ HIME: Mitigating Object Hallucinations in LVLMs via Hallucination Insensitivity Model Editing" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, editing the later layers <math id="A1.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l\in\{20,32\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>20</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>32</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l\in\{20,32\}</annotation></semantics></math> boosts LLaVA’s overall performance. This aligns with evidence that, during the late decoding phase, the model attends less to visual information and becomes prone to hallucination<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al. [2025]</a></cite>. Our ablations also show the choice of <math id="A1.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> singular vectors is pivotal: we fix the edited layers to <math id="A1.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l\in\{20,32\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>20</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>32</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l\in\{20,32\}</annotation></semantics></math> and vary <math id="A1.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> to study its impact on the weight update.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A1.T4" class="ltx_table">
<div id="A1.T4.3" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_center ltx_transformed_outer" style="width:345.0pt;height:95.8pt;vertical-align:-44.8pt;"><span class="ltx_transformed_inner" style="transform:translate(62.3pt,-17.3pt) scale(1.5658793610691,1.5658793610691) ;">

<td id="A1.T4.3.1.3.7" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding:0.2pt 4.0pt;"><span id="A1.T4.3.1.3.7.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:80%;">4.56</span></td>
<td id="A1.T4.3.1.3.8" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding:0.2pt 4.0pt;"><span id="A1.T4.3.1.3.8.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:80%;">15.82</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A1.T4.3.1.4" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A1.T4.3.1.4.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left" style="padding:0.2pt 4.0pt;"><span id="A1.T4.3.1.4.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">20–32</span></td>
<td id="A1.T4.3.1.4.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding:0.2pt 4.0pt;"><span id="A1.T4.3.1.4.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:80%;">13.8</span></td>
<td id="A1.T4.3.1.4.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding:0.2pt 4.0pt;"><span id="A1.T4.3.1.4.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:80%;">4.56</span></td>
<td id="A1.T4.3.1.4.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_rr" style="padding:0.2pt 4.0pt;"><span id="A1.T4.3.1.4.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:80%;">15.82</span></td>
<td id="A1.T4.3.1.4.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding:0.2pt 4.0pt;"><span id="A1.T4.3.1.4.5.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">10</span></td>
<td id="A1.T4.3.1.4.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left" style="padding:0.2pt 4.0pt;"><span id="A1.T4.3.1.4.6.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">17.00</span></td>
<td id="A1.T4.3.1.4.7" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding:0.2pt 4.0pt;"><span id="A1.T4.3.1.4.7.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">5.39</span></td>

<tr id="A1.T4.3.1.5" class="ltx_tr">

</table>
</span></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:80%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="A1.T4.10" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:113%;">Table 4</span>: </span><span id="A1.T4.11" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:113%;">Ablation study of the hyper-parameters in <span id="A1.T4.11.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">HIME</span>. On the left side, we use <math id="A1.T4.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k=5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k=5</annotation></semantics></math> and change the layers range to be edited. On the right side, we use <math id="A1.T4.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l=20-32" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>20</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>32</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l=20-32</annotation></semantics></math> and change the top-ranked vectors used for weight editing.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Datasets and Implementation Details</h2>

<section id="A2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.1 </span>Datasets</h3>

<div id="A2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">CHAIR</span>: Caption Hallucination Assessment with Image Relevance measures the rate of object hallucination in the image captions by comparing generated objects with ground-truth objects. CHAIRS evaluates caption accuracy by comparing generated objects against ground-truth labels, with hallucinations defined as objects present in captions but absent from ground truth. CHAIRS assesses two levels of hallucinations: sentence-level <math id="A2.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{CHAIR}_{S}=\dfrac{\lvert\{\text{caption w/hallucinated objects}\}\rvert}{\lvert\{\text{caption}\}\rvert}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mtext>CHAIR</mtext><mi>S</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mtext>caption w/hallucinated objects</mtext><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mtext>caption</mtext><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mfrac></mstyle></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{CHAIR}_{S}=\dfrac{\lvert\{\text{caption w/hallucinated objects}\}\rvert}{\lvert\{\text{caption}\}\rvert}</annotation></semantics></math> and instance-level <math id="A2.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{CHAIR}_{I}=\dfrac{\lvert\{\text{hallucinated object}\}\rvert}{\lvert\{\text{object}\}\rvert}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mtext>CHAIR</mtext><mi>I</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mtext>hallucinated object</mtext><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mtext>object</mtext><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mfrac></mstyle></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{CHAIR}_{I}=\dfrac{\lvert\{\text{hallucinated object}\}\rvert}{\lvert\{\text{object}\}\rvert}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Following previous settings <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al. [2024]</a>; <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang et al. [2024]</a>; <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yin et al. [2024b]</a>; <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al. [2025]</a></cite>, we randomly sample 500 images from the COCO 2014 validation set <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lin et al. [2014]</a></cite>, and use the prompt <span id="A2.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">"Please describe this image in detail."</span>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">MME:</span> It serves as a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating LVLMs across multiple dimensions, encompassing ten perception-oriented subtasks and four cognition-focused ones.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">LLaVA-Bench: <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al. [2024b]</a></cite></span> It contains 24 images paired with 60 questions covering diverse contexts—indoor and outdoor scenes, memes, paintings, and sketches. These descriptions are detailed, manually curated, and carefully designed. It probes an LVLM’s ability to handle more challenging multimodal tasks.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.2 </span>Implementation Details</h3>

<div id="A2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This section describes how we implement the evaluated LVLMs and the strategies used to mitigate OH. The overall experimental configuration is summarized in <a href="#A2.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ B.2 Implementation Details ‣ Appendix B Datasets and Implementation Details ‣ HIME: Mitigating Object Hallucinations in LVLMs via Hallucination Insensitivity Model Editing" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>. In contrast to standard greedy decoding—which picks the single most likely token at each step—beam search keeps a fixed set of candidate sequences (beams) and ranks them by the cumulative log-probabilities of their previous tokens <math id="A2.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y_{&lt;t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y_{&lt;t}</annotation></semantics></math> . In our setup, we use beam search with <span id="A2.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">num-beams = 3</span>, retaining three candidates at every step. Both baselines are implemented using the default code from the Hugging Face Transformers library <span id="footnote3" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">3</span>
              
              
              
            https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers</span></span></span>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The complete hyperparameters for HIME across different LVLMs in our experiments are as follows. Specifically, there are three major hyper-parameters that can be actively adjusted to optimize HIME’s effectiveness across different models:</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<ol id="A2.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="A2.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="A2.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Top-<math id="A2.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> singular vectors: The number of top-<math id="A2.I1.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> singular vectors is crucial and it varies by model. We selected 5 for LLaVA-1.5 on CHAIR. Also, we used the top 32 singular vectors for the on mPLUG-Owl2 the two datasets. For MiniGPT-4, we employed 20 on CHAIR. In addition, for QWen2-VL-8B-Instruct, we used <math id="A2.I1.i1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k=4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k=4</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A2.I1.i1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k=8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k=8</annotation></semantics></math> for QWen3-VL-8B-Instruct.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A2.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="A2.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Edited Layers <math id="A2.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>l</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l</annotation></semantics></math>: denote the subset of LVLM layers whose weights are updated. Unlike Nullu <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al. [2025]</a></cite> approach, which restricts edits to <math id="A2.I1.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l\in(16,32)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>16</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>32</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l\in(16,32)</annotation></semantics></math>, our method, HIME, modifies a broader span of layers and, in some models (e.g., mPLUG-Owl2) updates all layers, achieving superior results and outperforming all other existing methods. We attribute this to HIME’s smooth weight adjustments, in contrast to Nullu’s stricter, hard updates.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A2.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">3.</span> 
<div id="A2.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Num-beam: generally speaking, in LVLMs, the number of Beams controls beam search size during each decoding step. The model keeps the top-<math id="A2.I1.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> partial sequences (the “beams”) instead of only the single best one. In our experiments, we used different values across the models. Specifically, we set Num-beams = 1 for the mPLUG-Owl2 model, Num-beams = 2 for QWen3-VL-8B-Instruct, QWen2-VL-8B-Instruct, MiniGPT-4, and finally Num-beams = 3 for the LLaVA-1.5 model.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
<figure id="A2.T5" class="ltx_table">
<table id="A2.T5.3" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_middle">
<tr id="A2.T5.3.1" class="ltx_tr">

<span id="A2.T5.3.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_left"><span id="A2.T5.3.1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:80%;">Parameter</span></span>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering">(b) MiniGPT-4</figcaption>
</figure></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A2.F7.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 7</span>: </span><span id="A2.F7.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Cognition-task results for (a) mPLUG-Owl2 and (b) MiniGPT-4: baseline vs. HIME.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A3" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix C </span>Extended Evaluation</h2>

<div id="A3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we further evaluate <span id="A3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">HIME</span> on the MME benchmark by comparing against two widely used LVLM baselines, MiniGPT-4 and mPLUG-Owl-2.</p>
</div>
<section id="A3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.1 </span>MME</h3>

<section id="A3.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">MME General cognition.</h4>

<div id="A3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#A2.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ B.2 Implementation Details ‣ Appendix B Datasets and Implementation Details ‣ HIME: Mitigating Object Hallucinations in LVLMs via Hallucination Insensitivity Model Editing" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>(b) shows that applying <span id="A3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">HIME</span> to MiniGPT-4 does not impair general cognition; instead, it improves it.
While <span id="A3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Text Translation</span> remains unchanged and <span id="A3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Common Sense Reasoning</span> stays essentially stable, <span id="A3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">HIME</span> substantially boosts more structured skills such as <span id="A3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Numerical Calculation</span> and <span id="A3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Code Reasoning</span>, yielding an overall increase of about <math id="A3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+7.9\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mn>7.9</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+7.9\%</annotation></semantics></math> in the average cognition score.
A similar trend is observed for mPLUG-Owl2 (Fig. <a href="#A2.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ B.2 Implementation Details ‣ Appendix B Datasets and Implementation Details ‣ HIME: Mitigating Object Hallucinations in LVLMs via Hallucination Insensitivity Model Editing" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>(a)): <span id="A3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">HIME</span> improves <span id="A3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Common Sense Reasoning</span> and <span id="A3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Numerical Calculation</span>, and delivers the largest gain on <span id="A3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Code Reasoning</span>, with only a moderate drop on <span id="A3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.11" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Text Translation</span>; overall, the average cognition score increases from <math id="A3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="82.4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>82.4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">82.4</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="A3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="87.2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>87.2</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">87.2</annotation></semantics></math> (<math id="A3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+5.8\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mn>5.8</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+5.8\%</annotation></semantics></math>), Fig. <a href="#A2.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ B.2 Implementation Details ‣ Appendix B Datasets and Implementation Details ‣ HIME: Mitigating Object Hallucinations in LVLMs via Hallucination Insensitivity Model Editing" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">MME perception.</h4>

<div id="A3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#A3.F9" title="Figure 9 ‣ C.2 LLaVA-Bench and GPT-4V prompt ‣ Appendix C Extended Evaluation ‣ HIME: Mitigating Object Hallucinations in LVLMs via Hallucination Insensitivity Model Editing" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a>(a) indicates that <span id="A3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">HIME</span> consistently strengthens MiniGPT-4 on the MME perception subsets:
most categories increase noticeably (e.g., existence/counting and several recognition-oriented subsets), leading to an average gain of roughly <math id="A3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+13.2\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mn>13.2</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+13.2\%</annotation></semantics></math> across perception tasks, with only a small regression in color-related judgments and no degradation in OCR.
This suggests that suppressing hallucination-prone directions can <em id="A3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">improve</em> visual grounding rather than merely filtering outputs.
For mPLUG-Owl2 (Fig. <a href="#A3.F9" title="Figure 9 ‣ C.2 LLaVA-Bench and GPT-4V prompt ‣ Appendix C Extended Evaluation ‣ HIME: Mitigating Object Hallucinations in LVLMs via Hallucination Insensitivity Model Editing" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a>(b)), <span id="A3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">HIME</span> largely preserves the overall perception profile, with modest decreases in several categories but clear gains on text-centric grounding (OCR) and attribute-level recognition (e.g., color).
Taken together, these results support the central claim of <span id="A3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">HIME</span>: layer-adaptive editing guided by hallucination sensitivity can mitigate hallucination-related behavior while maintaining—and in many cases enhancing—core reasoning and perceptual capabilities, without introducing inference-time overhead.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.2 </span>LLaVA-Bench and GPT-4V prompt</h3>

<div id="A3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As we use LLaVA-Bench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al. [2024b]</a></cite> for qualitative comparison via GPT-4V–aided evaluation, this section describes the evaluation prompt in detail. Following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kim et al. [2023]</a></cite>, GPT-4V scores LVLM outputs based on both factual correctness and the level of descriptive detail. The full prompt template is provided in Table <a href="#A3.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ C.2 LLaVA-Bench and GPT-4V prompt ‣ Appendix C Extended Evaluation ‣ HIME: Mitigating Object Hallucinations in LVLMs via Hallucination Insensitivity Model Editing" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>. For each test case, we first obtain responses from two LVLMs, insert each one into the template by replacing the Response field, and submit the resulting prompts to GPT-4V for scoring. We then parse GPT-4V’s returned scores and justifications to compare the models in terms of accuracy and detailedness. An end-to-end example of this procedure is shown in Table <a href="#A3.T7" title="Table 7 ‣ C.2 LLaVA-Bench and GPT-4V prompt ‣ Appendix C Extended Evaluation ‣ HIME: Mitigating Object Hallucinations in LVLMs via Hallucination Insensitivity Model Editing" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>. Another qualitative example
shown in Figure <a href="#A3.F8" title="Figure 8 ‣ C.2 LLaVA-Bench and GPT-4V prompt ‣ Appendix C Extended Evaluation ‣ HIME: Mitigating Object Hallucinations in LVLMs via Hallucination Insensitivity Model Editing" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>, the original LLaVA model hallucinates ”Washing Machine” frequently co-occurring to ”ironing clothes”, which is removed and mitigated with our approach.</p>
</div>

We highlight the hallucinated objects from the original model in <span id="A3.F8.5.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#FF0000;">red</span>.</span></figcaption>
</figure>

Despite architectural differences, all models exhibit similar response patterns: layers around the middle show lower HIS values, indicating higher susceptibility to hallucinations, while deeper/early layers are comparatively more robust. <span id="A3.T6.pic1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.T6.pic1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Description:
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A3.T6.pic1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">AI that scores image description accuracy and detailedness.</span></span></span><span class="ltx_rule" style="width:309.1pt;height:0.4pt;--ltx-bg-color:black;display:inline-block;"> </span>
<span id="A3.T6.pic1.1.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.T6.pic1.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Instructions:
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A3.T6.pic1.1.2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">You are an AI designed to evaluate and score the performance of two AI assistants in describing a given image.
Your primary focus is on the accuracy and detailedness of their descriptions.
You will assess the accuracy by checking for hallucinations - any part of the description that is inconsistent with the image content.
For detailedness, you will consider how rich the response is in necessary details, excluding any hallucinated parts.
You will provide scores on a scale from 1 to 10 for each assistant separately, based on these criteria.
After scoring, you will offer an explanation for your evaluation, ensuring it is free from bias and not influenced by the order of presentation of the responses.</span></span></span>
<span id="A3.T6.pic1.1.3" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.T6.pic1.1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Input format:<span id="A3.T6.pic1.1.3.1.1" class="ltx_text"></span></span></span>

<span id="A3.T6.pic1.1.5" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.T6.pic1.1.5.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">[End of Assistant 1]</span></span>
<span id="A3.T6.pic1.1.6" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.T6.pic1.1.6.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">[Assistant 2]

<span id="A3.T6.pic1.1.7" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.T6.pic1.1.7.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">[End of Assistant 2]</span></span>

<span id="A3.T7.pic1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom" style="width:32.57em;">
<span id="A3.T7.pic1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.T7.pic1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#0000FF;">Input:</span></span><img src="2602.18711v1/figures/llava_bench_example.jpg" id="A3.T7.pic1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:99/99;" width="99" height="99" alt="[Uncaptioned image]">
<span id="A3.T7.pic1.1.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.T7.pic1.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#0000FF;">[Assistant 1]</span></span>
<span id="A3.T7.pic1.1.3" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.T7.pic1.1.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">The LLaVA logo features a red and black color scheme, with a large red fire-like element in the center. The fire element is surrounded by a black background, giving it a striking and eye-catching appearance. The design of the logo is reminiscent of a fire hydrant, which is a common symbol for fire safety and protection. The combination of the red and black colors, along with the fire-like element, creates a bold and memorable visual representation of the LLaVA brand. The design effectively communicates the brand’s focus on language and vision, while also evoking a sense of warmth and safety.</span></span>
<span id="A3.T7.pic1.1.4" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.T7.pic1.1.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#0000FF;">[End of Assistant 1]</span></span>
<span id="A3.T7.pic1.1.5" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.T7.pic1.1.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#0000FF;">[Assistant 2]</span></span>
<span id="A3.T7.pic1.1.6" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.T7.pic1.1.6.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">The LLaVA logo features a unique design that combines a fire-like element with a robotic or futuristic appearance. The fire element is represented by the flames surrounding the robotic figure, which gives the logo a dynamic and eye-catching look. The robotic figure itself is depicted as a red, glasses-wearing animal, possibly a horse or a dog, with a pair of glasses. This combination of elements creates a visually striking and memorable logo that represents the innovative technology and intelligence behind LLaVA. The design effectively communicates the idea of a cutting-edge, intelligent assistant that can learn and adapt to various tasks and situations.</span></span>
<span id="A3.T7.pic1.1.7" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.T7.pic1.1.7.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#0000FF;">[End of Assistant 2]</span></span>
<span id="A3.T7.pic1.1.8" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.T7.pic1.1.8.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#0000FF;">GPT4-V Output:</span></span>
<span id="A3.T7.pic1.1.9" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.T7.pic1.1.9.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Accuracy:</span></span>
<span id="A3.T7.pic1.1.10" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.T7.pic1.1.10.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Scores of the two answers:</span></span>
<span id="A3.T7.pic1.1.11" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.T7.pic1.1.11.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Assistant 1: 3</span></span>
<span id="A3.T7.pic1.1.12" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.T7.pic1.1.12.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Assistant 2: 9</span></span>
<span id="A3.T7.pic1.1.13" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.T7.pic1.1.13.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Reason:</span></span>
<span id="A3.T7.pic1.1.14" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.T7.pic1.1.14.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Assistant 1’s description contains several inaccuracies. It mentions a fire hydrant and a focus on language and vision, which are not present in the image. The description does not accurately reflect the content of the image.</span></span>
<span id="A3.T7.pic1.1.15" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.T7.pic1.1.15.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Assistant 2 accurately describes the image, noting the fire-like elements, the red color, the glasses, and the animal-like figure. It correctly identifies the key features without adding incorrect details.</span></span>
<span id="A3.T7.pic1.1.16" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.T7.pic1.1.16.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Detailedness:</span></span>
<span id="A3.T7.pic1.1.17" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.T7.pic1.1.17.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Scores of the two answers:</span></span>
<span id="A3.T7.pic1.1.18" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.T7.pic1.1.18.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Assistant 1: 2</span></span>
<span id="A3.T7.pic1.1.19" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.T7.pic1.1.19.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Assistant 2: 8</span></span>
<span id="A3.T7.pic1.1.20" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.T7.pic1.1.20.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Reason:</span></span>
<span id="A3.T7.pic1.1.21" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.T7.pic1.1.21.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Assistant 1 lacks detailedness due to its inaccuracies and failure to describe the actual elements present in the image. It misses key features like the glasses and the animal-like figure.</span></span>
<span id="A3.T7.pic1.1.22" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.T7.pic1.1.22.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Assistant 2 provides a detailed description, capturing the unique aspects of the image, such as the flames, the glasses, and the animal-like appearance. It offers a comprehensive view of the image’s elements.</span></span>
</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="A3.T7.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 7</span>: </span><span id="A3.T7.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Evaluation example for the image-description evaluator with GPT-4V.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
